Aerosol cans store propellant at several bars so the spray stays strong until the container is nearly empty. Warming the can raises internal pressure, which is why safety labels warn against heat and fire. The number is typical for room-temperature consumer spray cans. It is an overpressure relative to ambient conditions.

Airplane cabins are pressurized to an equivalent altitude of two to three kilometers, which is lower than sea level but comfortable for most passengers. The compromise reduces structural stress and weight while keeping oxygen levels acceptable. Sensitive travelers feel mild headache or fatigue at these numbers. The value is a typical cruise cabin pressure.

Sterilizing autoclaves run above atmospheric pressure so water can stay liquid at temperatures high enough to kill hardy microbes and spores. Laboratories and hospitals rely on this extra pressure every day, even though the absolute number is modest by engineering standards. The value is a standard operating overpressure for steam sterilization.

Road bicycles run far above car-tire pressure because their contact patches are small and rolling resistance matters. Riders trade comfort against pinch-flat resistance and speed by adjusting within this range. A floor pump gauge makes the number feel ordinary even though it is several atmospheres. The value is for a narrow road tire.

Near a black hole, pressures defined in usual material terms become meaningless as spacetime curvature dominates. Still, models of accretion disks describe effective pressures that are astronomical. Observations of x ray spectra inform these estimates. The value here is illustrative of those extremes.

Inside an engine cylinder during compression and combustion, gas pressure rises by orders of magnitude above the atmosphere around the vehicle. Pistons, rings, and head gaskets are all built around surviving this repeated load. The value here is a representative peak cylinder pressure for a gasoline engine rather than a diesel.

Champagne and other sparkling wines keep dissolved carbon dioxide under several bars of pressure inside the bottle. That is why corks eject so energetically when restraint is removed. Temperature matters strongly because dissolved gas and headspace both respond to warming. The number is a common room-temperature bottle pressure.

At one kilometer below the ocean surface, hydrostatic pressure reaches about ten megapascals. That is a hundred times sea-level atmospheric pressure pressing on every viewport, seal, and instrument housing. Deep-ocean vehicles live or die by whether they keep this number outside. The value is a round figure for 1000 meters depth.

Four kilometers down in the ocean, hydrostatic pressure reaches tens of megapascals and turns every seal, viewport, and cable into a deep-sea engineering problem. That is why remotely operated vehicles and abyssal landers look so overbuilt. Marine biology at this depth is inseparable from pressure adaptation. The value is a round-number benchmark for abyssal water.

Between galaxies, particle densities are so low that mechanical pressure approaches zero for human purposes. Radiation fields and magnetic stresses still act, but as a pressure they are vanishingly small. Spacecraft enjoy this quiet except when hit by solar storms. The value is an order of magnitude benchmark for deep space plasma pressure.

Deep in Earth’s mantle, carbon transforms into diamond under gigapascal class pressures and high temperatures. The combination stabilizes the crystal structure that sparkles on rings. Laboratory presses reproduce these conditions in tiny anvils. The value indicates the lower bound for natural formation.

Modern diesel injection systems atomize fuel by driving it through tiny nozzles at enormous pressure. That helps engines burn more cleanly and precisely, but it also makes leaks medically dangerous because fuel can penetrate skin. The number shows how far everyday automotive hardware reaches into high-pressure engineering. This value is a modern common-rail scale.

At Earth’s core, pressure from the overlying rock squeezes iron into exotic phases and drives a slowly convecting outer layer. Seismic waves reveal the magnitude indirectly. This pressure and temperature together power the geodynamo. The number is a standard estimate for the center.

At sea level on Earth, standard atmospheric pressure is about one hundred thousand pascals by definition. It sets boiling points, cooking times, and aircraft calibration. Weather systems drift a few percent above and below. The number is the canonical reference for pressure units.

Espresso machines use about nine bars of pressure to force hot water through compacted coffee grounds. That pressure is high enough to extract oils and emulsify crema in seconds rather than minutes. Home machines advertise it prominently because the number is part of the drink’s identity. The value is the classic brewing pressure target.

Systolic blood pressure in a healthy adult corresponds to this pressure difference in arteries during a heartbeat. The body regulates it with hormones and vessel elasticity. Long term elevations increase risk for stroke and heart disease. The number is a familiar medical baseline expressed in pascals.

A gentle human exhale produces only a few hundred pascals above ambient pressure, yet that is enough to move a column of air through the airway and across a flute or whistle. Respiratory therapists think in these small pressure differences when checking lung function. The number is for a calm, sustained breath rather than a forceful cough.

Industrial hydraulic systems routinely operate at tens to hundreds of bars to move heavy loads precisely. Hoses and fittings are rated well above working pressure to prevent catastrophic sprays. Small leaks feel deceptively gentle but can inject fluid into skin. The number is a mid range for shop presses and lifts.

Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles store hydrogen at around seven hundred bar, high enough that the tank becomes a sophisticated pressure vessel rather than a simple container. Composite wrapping and careful valve design make the system practical. The number shows how advanced transport already lives in the same pressure regime as industrial gas work. It is a standard automotive storage pressure.

A hyperbaric chamber used for diving medicine runs at a few atmospheres to treat decompression sickness. Breathing pure oxygen at these pressures accelerates nitrogen washout. Operators monitor for oxygen toxicity risks. The value is a representative treatment pressure.

Ultra high vacuum chambers in surface physics reach pressures near this value after long pumping and bakeout. Molecules arrive so rarely that clean crystal faces can be studied for minutes before contamination. Leak checking becomes an art at these numbers. The figure represents a good day on a research instrument.

At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the weight of nearly eleven kilometers of water piles up a crushing pressure. Only specialized research vessels and adapted organisms operate here. Material imperfections become critical under such loads. The number gives the scale at the deepest natural point on Earth.

On the Martian surface the thin atmosphere presses at only a few hundred pascals, less than one percent of Earth sea level. Water boils at body temperature under such conditions without a suit. Weather there is driven by dust, not by dense air. The number is for a typical day at the equator.

At the summit of Mount Everest the atmosphere pushes at only about a third of sea-level pressure. That thin air is why climbers need acclimatization and often supplemental oxygen. Water boils at a lower temperature there as well, changing cooking and physiology together. The number is a representative summit pressure.

Matter inside a neutron star is compressed beyond atomic structure, reaching pressures that defy ordinary materials science. Equations of state are constrained by astronomy rather than laboratory tests. The crust behaves like a bizarre ceramic under these loads. The number situates this extreme on the pressure scale.

At one hundred meters in the ocean, divers and submersibles face about ten times atmospheric pressure from the water column. Steel hulls and polymer seals are sized with generous safety margins. Breathing gas composition must change to avoid nitrogen narcosis. The value is a round figure for this depth.

A pressure cooker increases internal pressure modestly so water boils hotter and dinner finishes faster. Safety valves and lids are engineered against accidental opening under load. Recipes account for altitude and cooker setting. The number is for a common kitchen unit at operating pressure.

A scuba tank stores breathing gas at pressures high enough that a modest steel or aluminum cylinder can hold hours of underwater air. Regulators exist to step this down safely in stages. Divers think of the tank as ordinary gear, but the pressure inside belongs solidly in industrial territory. The value is a common fill pressure.

A typical can of carbonated soda holds an overpressure relative to air that keeps bubbles dissolved. Warming the can raises this pressure and makes foaming more likely on opening. Manufacturers choose levels to balance fizz and safety. The value is for a chilled sealed can.

The solar core carries stupendous pressure that enables fusion by pushing nuclei close despite their repulsion. Energy leaks outward over hundreds of thousands of years as heat and light. Surface storms above are gentle by comparison. The value is the order of magnitude for models of the Sun’s interior.

The water above you in a swimming pool adds pressure linearly with depth, so a few meters already feels on your ears. Lungs equalize by pushing air into sinuses, a skill every diver learns. Lifeguards know headaches often come from poor equalization rather than chlorine. The number is for a depth of two meters.

A passenger car tire is inflated to a few bars over atmospheric pressure to balance grip, wear, and comfort. Underinflation wastes fuel and overheats sidewalls, while overinflation reduces contact patch. Temperature changes during driving shift the number significantly. The value is for a warm tire after highway travel.

A household vacuum cleaner creates suction by lowering pressure below room air at the nozzle. The resulting pressure difference over a modest area is what actually lifts dust and grit. Motor noise tends to obscure how small the pressure number really is compared with industrial systems. The value is a representative static suction.

Venus wears a blanket of carbon dioxide so thick that the surface experiences pressures dozens of times higher than Earth. Metals soften and electronics require special cooling even before the heat is considered. Probes survive only hours with heroic engineering. The value is for the mean surface under cloud cover.

Water-jet cutters slice stone and metal by focusing water at hundreds of megapascals through a jewel orifice. The jet’s power comes less from heat than from the extreme local pressure and speed. Workshops treat the system with the same respect as explosive tooling. The value is a representative cutting-head pressure.

Masonry design often treats whole walls rather than brick alone, but the brick material itself lives in the low tens of gigapascals. That is enough to keep arches and facades from sagging visibly under ordinary loads. The value is a representative engineering brick modulus.

Unidirectional carbon fiber composites have an effective modulus near two hundred gigapascals along the fiber direction, while transverse is far lower. Rule of mixtures gives a first estimate based on fiber volume. Layup choices tailor stiffness to load paths. The number is for a high modulus fiber epoxy lamina.

Cartilage combines a collagen network with pressurized water to form a poroelastic material with low instantaneous modulus. Under sustained load the modulus rises as fluid drains. Healthy joints depend on this time dependence for shock absorption. The value is an initial small strain tangent.

Engineering ceramics achieve very high modulus due to strong ionic and covalent bonds. Their stiffness remains high even at heat where metals soften. Designers trade brittleness against this stiffness for cutting tools. The value is for alumina.

Concrete’s modulus depends on aggregate and curing; it is not a pure material constant. Codes use empirical formulas tied to compressive strength. Long term creep lowers effective stiffness in service. The value is a short term tangent for a structural mix.

Copper combines excellent electrical conduction with a modulus a bit above one hundred gigapascals, enough to make busbars and springs hold form while still yielding more readily than steels. Purity and cold work change strength much more than stiffness. That separation is why electrical and mechanical design tables both matter. The value is a representative modulus for bulk copper.

Cork compresses easily at first because gas-filled cells collapse and recover, which is why it works so well as a bottle stopper and vibration isolator. Its modulus is far above a liquid but far below wood or plastic. Moisture and direction both matter because the cell structure is anisotropic. The value is a representative small-strain modulus.

Diamond is among the stiffest known solids because of its dense sp3 network. Small strains store huge elastic energy before fracture. Microelectromechanical resonators exploit this for high frequency stability. The value is a polycrystalline average.

Polymer foams behave like springs in a scaffold of cells, so their effective modulus is tiny until densification. Cell size, gas content, and skin layers matter as much as chemistry. Designers tune this for pillows versus helmet liners. The value is for a flexible open cell foam in small strain compression.

Glass is relatively stiff with a modulus similar to some metals despite brittleness. Defects control strength but not this initial slope. Temperature near the glass transition softens it dramatically. The value is for soda lime glass at room temperature.

Graphene’s in plane modulus approaches the theoretical limit for a two dimensional lattice. Out of plane bending is much softer, illustrating geometric effects. Large area films reduce modulus due to wrinkles and defects. The value is from nanoindentation on monolayers.

Water ice is much less stiff than rock or metal but far stiffer than rubber, which is why glaciers can support cracks and transmit seismic waves even while creeping over years. Planetary scientists rely on this modulus when modeling icy moons and ice shelves. Temperature shifts it meaningfully. The value is a typical terrestrial ice modulus.

Kevlar fibers are less stiff than carbon fibers but still very much engineering fibers, landing around tens of gigapascals in axial modulus. Their real advantage is the combination of stiffness, toughness, and low density. Ballistic fabrics and ropes turn that combination into practical products. The value is a representative fiber-direction modulus.

Lead is soft in yield strength but not infinitely floppy: its elastic modulus still sits in the tens of gigapascals. That is why lead pipes and sheets can hold shape until creep and plasticity take over. The contrast between low modulus metals and high modulus ceramics is one of the simplest material lessons to feel by hand. The value is a standard handbook number.

Magnesium alloys are attractive in vehicles and aircraft because their stiffness is lower than aluminum’s but their density is lower too. That means components can still achieve respectable specific stiffness when geometry is optimized. Corrosion protection and fatigue remain important design constraints. The value is a representative modulus for structural magnesium alloys.

The crust of a neutron star has a colossal effective shear modulus in models, reflecting interactions in a dense nuclear lattice. Starquakes excite oscillations that encode this stiffness indirectly. Laboratory analogies are qualitative at best. The value is an estimate from astrophysical constraints.

Nylon sits in the low-gigapascal range, stiff enough for gears, fasteners, and bushings yet compliant enough to damp shock and noise. Moisture softens it because water acts as a plasticizer in the polymer network. That is why dry and conditioned values can differ noticeably in datasheets. The value is a representative small-strain modulus for nylon 6.

Hardwoods like oak are stiffer than many softwoods because of their denser microstructure and higher latewood fraction. Furniture makers and structural engineers both feel this directly in how little a board flexes under load. Grain direction still dominates the number, so this is an along-grain figure. The value is a representative modulus for oak.

PLA prints feel rigid because their elastic modulus reaches a few gigapascals, substantially above many household plastics. That helps small printed parts keep shape, though it does not guarantee toughness. Temperature softening remains the main weakness. The number is a representative modulus for solid PLA.

Polyethylene is flexible because its elastic modulus is only a few hundred megapascals, several hundred times lower than common metals. That makes it ideal for bottles, cutting boards, and films that need to bend without cracking. Crystallinity shifts the stiffness a bit but not the basic scale. The value is representative for HDPE.

Soft rubber stores little energy per strain because chains uncoil easily, leading to a very low modulus. As strain rises, entropic elasticity stiffens the response. Fillers like carbon black raise the modulus by reinforcing the network. The value given is for an unfilled gum rubber at room temperature.

Silica aerogel is often called solid smoke because its density is so low and its stiffness is only modestly above that of soft foams. Even so, it is a true solid with a measurable elastic slope that matters in insulation panels and particle collectors. Large strains quickly move it beyond the small-strain regime. The value is a representative low-density aerogel modulus.

Crystalline silicon is the structural backbone of chips and MEMS, and its modulus is high enough that tiny beams and resonators can ring at precise frequencies. The exact value depends on crystal direction because the lattice is anisotropic. Semiconductor fabrication treats this as a design parameter, not trivia. The number is a representative orientation-averaged modulus.

Silicon carbide combines ceramic hardness with very high elastic stiffness, making it valuable for armor, abrasives, mirrors, and high-temperature components. Components made from it resist small elastic strain strongly before brittle failure becomes the real limit. It is a good reminder that stiffness and toughness are separate traits. The value is a representative engineering modulus.

Spider dragline silk stretches more than most engineering fibers, but its modulus still lands around tens of gigapascals, high enough to store useful elastic energy in a light thread. Biologists care because that balance of stiffness and toughness is rare in natural materials. Humidity changes the feel quickly. The value is a representative dry-fiber modulus.

Steels cluster near two hundred gigapascals in modulus across many alloys and tempers. Heat treatment alters yield and toughness but not this slope much. That is why beams deflect similarly before yield regardless of grade. The value is the canonical handbook number.

Tendon stores elastic energy for locomotion with a modulus around a gigapascal that rises with strain. Warm tissues display higher extensibility and lower stiffness initially. Training induces remodeling that tunes this property. The figure is a small strain slope for Achilles tendon.

Titanium alloys are roughly half as stiff as steel at similar densities, giving good specific stiffness. Designers exploit this for weight sensitive parts that must flex without yielding. Temperature and phase mix set exact values. The number is for Ti 6Al 4V.

Tungsten is one of the stiffest practical metals, which is why it holds shape at heat and finds use in filaments, weights, and tooling. Its density is famous, but the high modulus is just as important in applications that need resistance to elastic bending. Brittleness is the tradeoff. The value is a representative room-temperature modulus.

Softwoods are anisotropic; along the grain the modulus is moderate, across the grain it is an order lower. Moisture acts like a plasticizer that reduces stiffness. Builders season wood to stabilize this property. The value is longitudinal for dried spruce.
